chapters.name: Chapter 1: How robots and automation work

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Robots, automation and AI: what is the difference?
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Sort real machines into robots, automation and AI, and explain sense-think-act.
This lesson builds toward: Given examples of real machines, you will identify which are robots, which are automation and which use AI, and describe the sense-think-act loop, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Automation means a machine or program does a task on its own once it is set up, like a dishwasher cycle or a factory conveyor. A robot is a machine that can sense the world around it and move or act in it, like a robot vacuum or a warehouse robot that carries shelves.
Every robot follows the same loop: sense, think, act. It senses with sensors (cameras, bump switches, distance sensors), thinks with a computer program that decides what to do, and acts with motors, wheels, arms or grippers. Then it senses again.
AI is a kind of thinking program that learns patterns from examples, such as spotting a person in a camera image. Many robots use simple rules, not AI. Some use AI to see, plan routes or understand speech.
Words to know:
- Automation: a machine or program doing a task on its own once set up.
- Robot: a machine that can sense its surroundings and act in them.
- Sense-think-act: the loop every robot follows: take in information, decide, then move or act.
- AI: artificial intelligence: programs that learn patterns from examples to make decisions.
Try it now: Pick three machines you have seen (for example a robot vacuum, a self-checkout, a delivery drone). For each, write whether it is automation or a robot, and one way it senses, thinks and acts.
You can now tell automation, robots and AI apart and describe any robot using sense-think-act.

check.q: What does a robot do in the "act" step of sense-think-act?
options: Moves or does something with motors, wheels or grippers
Decides what to do with a program
check.why: Acting means moving or doing something with motors, wheels, arms or grippers.

check.q: A friend says every robot uses AI. What do you tell them?
options: That is right; robots cannot work without AI
AI means a robot has wheels
Many robots follow simple rules; only some use AI
Robots and AI are the same thing
check.why: Many robots use simple rules; some use AI to see, plan routes or understand speech.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Sensors and actuators: the robot's senses and muscles
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Match common sensors and actuators to the jobs they do.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job a robot must do, you will choose the sensors and actuators it needs, with a reason for each part.
Sensors are a robot's senses. A distance sensor measures how far away something is. A bump sensor knows when the robot touches something. A camera sees images. A line or color sensor sees the floor. A GPS unit knows location outdoors.
Actuators are a robot's muscles: anything that makes it move or act. Motors turn wheels, servos turn joints to an exact angle, and grippers or suction cups pick things up.
When designing a robot, start with the job. A robot that must stop before hitting a wall needs a distance or bump sensor and drive motors. A robot that sorts red and blue boxes needs a color sensor and a gripper.
Words to know:
- Sensor: a part that takes in information, like distance, touch, light or images.
- Actuator: a part that makes the robot move or act, like a motor or gripper.
- Servo: a motor that turns to an exact angle.
Try it now: Design on paper a robot for one job, such as watering plants or carrying a box across a room. List the sensors and actuators it needs and why.
You can now choose the sensors and actuators a robot needs for a job.

check.why: Actuators make the robot move or act; a gripper picks things up.

check.q: You are designing a robot that follows a black line on the floor. Which sensor do you add?
check.why: A line or color sensor looks at the floor and can follow a line.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing an algorithm before you code
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a step-by-step plan with a loop and a decision that a robot could follow.
This lesson builds toward: Given a robot task, you will write an algorithm in plain words with exact steps, a loop and an if-then decision, so it works when you walk through it yourself.
An algorithm is a list of exact steps to finish a task. Robots cannot guess, so every step must be clear: "drive forward 50 centimeters" instead of "go a bit".
Two tools make algorithms powerful. A loop repeats steps, such as "repeat 4 times: drive forward, turn right 90 degrees" to drive a square. A decision, also called an if-then, chooses what to do: "if the wall is closer than 10 centimeters, then stop; otherwise keep driving".
Write it in plain words or draw a flowchart first. Then walk through it yourself as if you were the robot. If you bump into something on paper, the robot will too.
Step by step:
- Write the goal in one sentence.
- List each step in order, with exact amounts.
- Look for steps that repeat and turn them into a loop.
- Add any if-then decisions that use a sensor.
- Walk through it yourself to test it.
Words to know:
- Algorithm: a list of exact steps to finish a task.
- Loop: a set of steps that repeats.
- If-then: a decision: if something is true, do one thing; otherwise do another.
- Flowchart: a drawing of an algorithm with boxes and arrows.
Try it now: Write an algorithm, with a loop, for a robot to drive in a square. Then add an if-then step so it stops if something is in its way. Walk through it with a toy, a phone or your own feet.
You can now write a clear algorithm with a loop and an if-then decision, and test it on paper.

check.q: What does a loop do in an algorithm?
check.why: A loop repeats steps, like driving forward and turning four times for a square.

check.q: Your plan says "go a bit forward". What do you change before coding?
options: Give an exact amount, like 50 centimeters
check.why: Robots cannot guess, so every step needs an exact amount.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Coding a virtual robot with blocks
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Open a free virtual robot and code it to drive a square.
This lesson builds toward: Using a free virtual robot tool such as VEXcode VR, you will code the robot with blocks to drive a square, so it returns close to where it started.
You can practice robot coding in a web browser with no robot. VEXcode VR, from VEX Robotics, has a free version that uses drag-and-drop blocks, like Scratch, and runs on computers, Chromebooks and tablets at vr.vex.com. Other free options exist; your school or library may have one it prefers.
Blocks snap together like puzzle pieces. A "drive forward" block moves the robot, a "turn right" block turns it, and a "repeat" block makes a loop. You press Start to watch the robot follow your program in a virtual playground.
Turn your paper algorithm into blocks one step at a time. Run it after each change so you know which block caused what.
Step by step:
- Open vr.vex.com in a web browser.
- Pick a simple playground with open floor space.
- Drag a drive-forward block and a turn-right block into the program.
- Wrap them in a repeat block set to 4.
- Press Start and watch. Adjust the distance or turn until it drives a clean square.
Words to know:
- Block coding: programming by snapping visual blocks together instead of typing code.
- Playground: the virtual space where the simulated robot drives.
- Simulator: software that acts like a real machine so you can practice safely.
Official sources:
- VEX Robotics: VEXcode VR
Try it now: In VEXcode VR or another free virtual robot, code the robot to drive a square using a repeat block. Get it to finish close to where it started.
You can now code a virtual robot with blocks, using a loop to drive a square.

check.q: In block coding, what does the Start button do?
options: Saves your program to a USB stick
Runs the program so you can watch the robot follow it
check.why: Pressing Start runs the program in the virtual playground.

check.q: You added five new blocks at once and the robot crashes. What should you have done?
options: Run the program after each change
check.why: Running after each change shows which block caused what.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Using a sensor to decide, then debugging
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Add a sensor-based if-then to a robot program and fix a bug.
This lesson builds toward: Given a robot that must avoid a wall, you will add a sensor-based if-then to the program and fix at least one bug, changing one thing at a time until the robot stops and turns at the wall.
A robot that only follows fixed steps is blind. Add a sensor and it can react. In block coding, you use an "if" block with a sensor reading inside, such as "if distance is less than 100 millimeters".
A common pattern: forever loop, inside it an if-then-else. If the wall is close, stop and turn. Else, drive forward. The robot checks the sensor again and again, which is the sense-think-act loop in code.
Bugs are normal. Debugging means finding and fixing them. Change one thing at a time, run it, and watch. Common bugs: the turn is not quite 90 degrees, the distance number is in the wrong unit, or a block sits outside the loop.
Step by step:
- Add a forever loop.
- Inside it, add an if-then-else block.
- Put a distance sensor check in the if.
- Then: stop and turn. Else: drive forward.
- Run it, watch for a mistake, change one thing, run it again.
Words to know:
- Bug: a mistake in a program that makes it act wrongly.
- Debugging: finding and fixing bugs.
- Forever loop: a loop that keeps repeating until the program is stopped.
Try it now: Code the robot to drive forward until its distance sensor finds a wall, then stop, turn and keep going. Write down one bug you hit and how you fixed it.
You can now use a sensor reading in an if-then-else to make a robot react, and debug the program.

check.q: In the wall-avoiding program, why use a forever loop?
options: So the robot keeps checking the sensor again and again
So the robot only checks once
So the robot drives a square
check.why: The forever loop repeats the sensor check, which is sense-think-act in code.

check.q: Your robot stops 1 meter from the wall instead of close to it. What is a likely bug?
options: The robot needs a new battery
The distance number is in the wrong unit
check.why: A distance in the wrong unit, like centimeters instead of millimeters, is a common bug.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Where robots work, and working safely with them
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name real robot jobs and the safety rules people follow around robots.
This lesson builds toward: Given a workplace that uses robots, you will name real robot jobs and the safety rules people follow around robots, naming at least two jobs and two safety rules.
Robots and automation are used in warehouses (moving shelves and packages), factories (welding, packing), farms (milking, spraying, drones), hospitals (delivering supplies, assisting surgeons) and the military (bomb disposal, unmanned aircraft).
People still do important jobs: robotics technicians fix and maintain robots, operators run and watch them, and programmers and engineers design them. Many technician jobs start with a community college certificate or military training.
Safety comes first. Industrial robots can move fast and hit hard. Workers keep out of marked robot areas, use the emergency stop, and lock out power before maintenance. Collaborative robots, or cobots, are designed to work closer to people, but the same rule applies: follow the site's safety training.
Words to know:
- Robotics technician: a person who installs, maintains and repairs robots.
- Cobot: a collaborative robot built to work near people.
- Emergency stop: a big button that stops a machine right away.
Try it now: Final task: finish your square program and your sensor program in the virtual robot tool, fix at least one bug, and write three sentences explaining what your robot senses, how it decides and how it acts.
You can now code a virtual robot that senses and reacts, explain how it works, and name real robot jobs and safety rules.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Square program The robot does not drive a square, or the program has no loop. A repeat block drives the robot in a square that ends close to the start. The distance and turn were adjusted so the square is clean and even. Wall-avoiding program The robot hits the wall or never moves again. A forever loop with an if-then-else: it stops and turns at the wall, then keeps driving. It works from more than one starting spot in the playground. Testing and debugging No bug was found or fixed. At least one bug was found and fixed by changing one thing at a time. Can explain what caused the bug and how they found it. Plan before code No written plan, or steps like "go a bit". A plain-words plan with exact steps, a loop and an if-then. The plan was walked through on paper and fixed before coding. Sense, think, act explained The three sentences are missing or do not name a sensor. Three sentences say what the robot senses, how it decides and how it acts. Also says whether the robot uses AI or simple rules, and why. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Who fixes and maintains robots at a factory or warehouse?
check.why: Robotics technicians fix and maintain robots.

check.q: You are touring a warehouse and see robots moving behind a marked line. What do you do?
options: Step over the line to look closer
Touch a robot to see if it stops
Stay out of the marked area and follow the guide's safety rules
check.why: Industrial robots can move fast and hit hard, so people stay out of marked robot areas.
